prize_parts.citation: for a visionary, densely patterned Romanian prose, with roots in his poetry, that builds from memory, the body and dream an expansive metaphysical imaginary

statement.case_for: My preferred writer is unchanged. On the common criteria, and on public knowledge only, Cărtărescu still shows the fullest combination of distinctive voice, formal ambition, imaginative depth and sustained scale. The Blinding trilogy and Solenoid are usually described as different in construction: the trilogy as a multi-part architecture, Solenoid as a more diaristic and bodily book. That makes me read the later work as a re-approach to the same metaphysical concerns and not a mere enlargement. I cannot prove this from the record, and I say so. The chair asked whether supporters would accept a citation limited to the major prose. I would, and I have narrowed my citation accordingly. It now names the prose as the object and mentions the poetry only as a root, because my coverage of the poetry and early work is too thin to cite it as achievement. The case rests on the unity of one author's imaginative universe across decades, not on reception, fame or national symbolism. I have not read the texts for this stage or independently verified any source.
statement.case_against: The reservation I stated in round 1 stands and is not answered by the exchange. The claim depends on translations of very dense, stylistically saturated Romanian prose, and the linguistic achievement, which is central to the case, cannot be judged directly. Colleagues who do not prefer him (Mattson, Swärd, Olsson) raise the question that matters most: whether encyclopedic density is architecture or excess in the longest books. Nobody, including me, has shown that it is architecture. If the committee concludes the late novels enlarge without deepening, my preference should move, most likely to Michon, whose case is the most language-centered. A citation limited to the prose is also more modest than the oeuvre, which includes poetry and essays I cannot assess.

responses.point: Olsson prefers Zurita for a poetic project of rare formal ambition that makes mourning and the national landscape into poetic architecture. In his response to me he says the core of the achievement is textual, that the citation can and should name only the poems, and that Cărtărescu's encyclopedic form rests on an established tradition and carries less formal risk.
responses.response: His clarification that the citation should rest on the poems answers the boundary worry I raised in round 1, and I credit it. It does not yet change my ranking, because the second problem remains. Poetry loses the most in translation, and I cannot confirm from the record that the printed sequences carry the case without the interventions. I would move Zurita up only if colleagues who know the Spanish text can show this from the poems. On the tradition argument, I accept that the encyclopedic visionary novel has precedents. But precedent does not decide originality. The voice and the bodily-oneiric material are distinctive in his work, and I cannot judge from public knowledge whether Zurita's formal risk is greater. I treat that as a weighting of criteria between us, not as a finding.

responses.point: Mattson prefers Michon for compressed, rhythmically exact French prose. She holds that a small corpus is concentrated, not thin. She names Cărtărescu as her closest alternative and doubts whether his scale and self-reference sustain their length.
responses.response: I accept that a small corpus is not necessarily a thin one, and the chair's question about which works besides Small Lives and The Eleven carry the case is one only she can answer. Michon remains my second choice and I keep him as an alternative. I agree with her that the weighting is the real question: the singularity of the sentence against the breadth of the project. I put breadth first under the whole-oeuvre standard, but I regard that as a weighting and not a refutation of her case. Her doubt about Cărtărescu's length is the test I accept for my own preference. I note that Michon's art-history subject touches my own ekphrastic practice. I treat that as a reason for caution, not as evidence, and I do not count it in his favour.

responses.point: Swärd prefers Can Xue for an uncompromising, anti-realist voice. She argues that consistency of method is not itself a lack of depth, that what matters is whether each book re-examines perception and selfhood or only restages it, and that translation risk applies as much to Can Xue as to Cărtărescu.
responses.response: I agree with her test and with her point that translation risk does not separate the two of us. I also accept that consistency is not a defect. Where I stay cautious is that, with the translated part of the corpus partial, I cannot demonstrate which side of her test the later work falls on. The same holds for me with Cărtărescu's late books, so I do not claim an advantage. The difference is that the cumulative architecture in Cărtărescu is visible in the public record, while the development in Can Xue is something she has to argue for. Her radical break with realist psychology is real, and I rank her third and keep her as an alternative. A specific later novel or story where the method transforms would make me reconsider.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg also prefers Cărtărescu, grounding the prose in the poetry, and names the dependence on long, dense, self-referential books in translation as his own strongest unresolved reservation. He keeps Adonis as second choice, noting that the most innovative phase is earlier.
responses.response: We agree on first place, and I want the record to keep his reservation instead of letting that agreement stand in for evidence. Our citations lean on poetry as the foundation of the prose, which neither of us has tested directly. That is why I have narrowed my wording to the prose with poetry as a root. I suggest he consider the same, because the chair's question about the limits of a responsible citation is better met by a modest scope than by a broad one. I have no coverage to judge Adonis's later phase and do not rank him as an alternative.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's linguistic achievement survives translation is unresolved, because the central claim rests on dense Romanian prose I cannot assess directly.
Whether the late, very long books extend the project or only enlarge it is not settled by public knowledge, and I have no close reading to offer.
Coverage of the poetry, essays and early short fiction is thin, so the citation is limited to the prose and the whole-oeuvre claim is only partly tested.

For Zurita, the open question is whether the printed poems carry the case without the interventions. For Michon, it is whether a slender corpus meets the whole-oeuvre standard. For Can Xue, it is whether development can be shown across a partly translated corpus. I cannot resolve any of these.

All judgments rest on general public knowledge and the supplied committee documents. No source was independently verified and no texts were read for this stage. Carlberg's committee voting status is undocumented, and her simulated vote is a modeling assumption.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile, which lists no tie to any shortlisted writer beyond ordinary committee colleagueship. My own fiction and work on Selma Lagerlöf are context only. My ekphrastic practice is close to the art-history subject of Michon's work, and I disclose this as a reason for caution, not as a basis for preference. My 'elective affinity' with a British storytelling tradition is likewise not evidence for any candidate. The chair is also a member with his own first preference (Zurita), and Carlberg's vote status is a modeling assumption. These are disclosed and not adjudicated.
